content.text: Intonation is the rise and fall of the voice to convey meaning or emotion.
It changes a sentence’s function (statement, question, emotion).
Different intonation patterns signal attitudes like surprise, irony, doubt, or certainty.
Say these aloud and decide if it sounds like a question or statement:
Listen to two different intonations for the sentence “Really?” — how does each one feel?
They have close meanings but are used differently in context.
We study them to speak and write with accuracy, avoiding awkward or incorrect choices.
She gave me some great ______ about my résumé.
“I actually live in São Paulo now.” → Use “currently” correctly.
Choose the word that sounds like “peace”:
I want a piece of cake.
– “Are you going to assist the meeting?”
– “Ah, right! I always mix those two.”
– “I want to pretend that I’m rich.”
– “Be careful! That doesn’t mean you want to plan to be rich.”
– “No article with ‘advice’ — it’s uncountable. Try: ‘some good advice.’”

Lucas moved to Canada and faced confusion with English words. One day, he told his professor, “I pretend to be a good student.” The professor laughed, explaining that “pretend” wasn’t the word he wanted. Another time, Lucas said, “Actually, I live in Toronto,” when he meant “currently.” These mistakes made him more careful. He started writing down similar words and their meanings. Eventually, he learned the difference between “advice” and “advise”, “peace” and “piece”, and even stopped mixing up “push” and “pull” on doors!
What were Lucas’s two main mistakes?
How did Lucas deal with confusing words?
Which similar words were mentioned in the text?
I pretend to visit France next year.
Choose the better option for clarity:
I want to (assist / attend) the workshop.
I’m (actually / currently) studying English in Canada.
Let’s go over (they’re / their / there) to say hello.
I went to the library and bought a book.
They want to pretend in this project.
He said me he was tired.
Which sentence uses the word correctly?
A. I gave him a great advise.
B. She advised me to be calm.
C. She said me to stay home.
D. Actually I’m married with a teacher.
Answer: B (Correct use of “advise” as a verb)
Similar words can confuse meaning, pronunciation, or both.
False friends cause unique problems for Portuguese speakers.
Choose based on context: meaning, collocation, tone.
Always double-check if the word really means what you think it does.
Write a paragraph using 5 sets of similar words correctly. Underline them.
Watch a video of common word confusions (e.g. Rachel’s English or BBC Learning English). Write down at least 5 pairs that confuse you.
Rewrite 10 incorrect sentences using false friends (you can search for typical errors Brazilians make with “actually”, “library”, etc.).
Record yourself explaining the difference between 3 pairs of similar words: “advice/advise”, “accept/except”, and “peace/piece”.
Write a dialogue between two people using at least 6 commonly confused words (e.g., “attend”, “pretend”, “currently”, “library”).
Create a short story where a character constantly uses the wrong word. Rewrite it at the end with the correct version.
